newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parties seek agreement on holding firms.
newsitem.headline: Japan parties seek agreement on holding firms.

text.p: Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and its allies will try to reach an agreement this week on lifting a decades-long ban on holding companies, an LDP official said on Wednesday.

An agreement between the LDP, the Social Democratic Party and the small Sakigake party would enable the government to work out necessary changes to Japan's anti-monopoly law and submit them to the current session of parliament by March 11, an official of the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) said.
The parties had been expected to reach an agreement on Thursday, but an LDP official quoted Taku Yamasaki, chairman of LDP's policy-making committee, as saying this would now be difficult.

One of the reasons for the delay was that the Japan Federation of Employers' Associations (Nikkeiren) and labour unions had not agreed on labour issues which may result from the lifting of the ban, he was quoted as saying.
He said he now wanted the three political parties to make utmost efforts to reach the agreement on Friday, the official said.
Jiji news agency quoted Nikkeiren chairman Jiro Nemoto as saying that holding companies were absolutely necessary to revitalise Japan's economy and ensure international competitiveness.
If submitted by March 11, the legislation could be passed in the current session ending in June and take effect early next year, the FTC official said.
U.S. Occupation forces introduced the ban on holding companies in 1947 to break up powerful conglomerates known as "zaibatsu" which the United States believed had contributed to Japan's war effort.
Big businesses and banks have demanded the ban be lifted to help them streamline and compete with overseas rivals.
Under draft legislation recently worked out by the FTC, three types of holding companies will continue to be banned to avoid an excessive concentration of business strength.
The three include extremely large corporate groups, corporate groups headed by a large financial institution, and groups formed by leading firms in the same or related industries.
